items.followUp: What is data sharing over a network?

rubric.why: Shows that file sharing involves making files available to others.
rubric.description: Defines file sharing as making files available to other users or devices.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining that files are shared or made accessible.

rubric.why: Identifies who or what can exchange the files.
rubric.description: Mentions users or computers connected through a network.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for mentioning users or networked computers.

modelAnswer: File sharing is the process of making files available to other users or computers.
It is commonly done over a network so that users can access or exchange files.

rubric.why: Identifies the shared connection used by multiple devices.
rubric.description: States that multiple devices use one communication link or channel.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying a shared link or channel.

rubric.why: Explains that the connection is shared among devices.
rubric.description: States that the devices share the connection.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining that the link or channel is shared.

modelAnswer: A multi-point connection is a connection in which two or more devices share a single communication link or channel.
The capacity of that link is shared among the connected devices.

items.followUp: Write the HTML tag used to set a web page's background colour.

rubric.why: Identifies the body element whose attribute sets the page background in basic HTML.
rubric.description: Uses the body tag.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming or writing the body tag.

rubric.why: Identifies the colour attribute or property.
rubric.description: Gives the bgcolor attribute or a CSS background-color property, with a colour value.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for giving a correct colour-setting attribute or property.

modelAnswer: In basic HTML, set the background colour by using the bgcolor attribute in the opening body tag.
Example: <body bgcolor="yellow">

items.followUp: What is a hyperlink, and how is it created in HTML?

rubric.why: States the purpose of an anchor: it creates a link.
rubric.description: Explains that an anchor is used to make a hyperlink.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying that an anchor creates a link.

rubric.why: Identifies a destination to which the link can lead.
rubric.description: States that the link can lead to another page, website, or location.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming a valid link destination.

modelAnswer: An anchor is used to create a hyperlink on a web page.
The hyperlink can take the user to another web page, website, or a location within the same page.

items.followUp: Explain time complexity and space complexity, using a simple algorithm as an example.

rubric.why: Identifies the time taken or number of operations as one measure of efficiency.
rubric.description: Explains that time efficiency is measured by execution time or the number of steps/operations.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly describing time efficiency.

rubric.why: Identifies memory use as another measure of efficiency.
rubric.description: Explains that space efficiency is measured by the memory used.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly describing space efficiency.

rubric.why: Provides a relevant algorithm as an example.
rubric.description: Uses a suitable example such as linear search through a list.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for giving a relevant algorithm example.

rubric.why: Connects the example to how its resource use grows with input size.
rubric.description: Explains that linear search may check up to n items (time O(n)); alternatively, gives a correct resource estimate for the example.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct efficiency estimate linked to the example.

modelAnswer: An algorithm's efficiency is measured by the time it takes to run and the memory space it uses.
Time efficiency can be described by counting the steps or operations performed as the input size grows.
Space efficiency is described by the amount of memory used as the input size grows.
For example, a linear search through n items may make up to n comparisons, so its time complexity is O(n).

items.followUp: Why should you avoid using personal information in a password?

rubric.why: Recognizes that a password should be sufficiently long.
rubric.description: Recommends using a long password, preferably at least eight characters.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that passwords should be long.

rubric.why: Identifies the use of varied letter cases.
rubric.description: Recommends mixing uppercase and lowercase letters.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for mentioning mixed letter case.

rubric.why: Identifies digits as a useful character type.
rubric.description: Recommends including numbers or digits.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for mentioning numbers.

rubric.why: Recognizes added character variety or avoidance of easy-to-guess personal details.
rubric.description: Recommends special characters/symbols and avoiding easily guessed personal information.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for mentioning symbols or avoiding personal details.

modelAnswer: A good password should be long, preferably at least eight characters.
It should mix uppercase and lowercase letters.
It should include numbers and special characters or symbols.
It should not contain easily guessed personal information, such as a name or birth date.

items.followUp: What are the 5Ws used to gather information about an event?

rubric.why: Identifies the five questions used to gather complete information.
rubric.description: Lists the 5Ws: who, what, when, where, and why.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly naming the 5Ws.

rubric.why: Shows the purpose of using the 5Ws.
rubric.description: Explains that the 5Ws help gather key or complete information about an event or topic.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating their information-gathering purpose.

modelAnswer: The 5Ws are Who, What, When, Where, and Why.
They are questions used to gather the key information about an event or topic.

items.followUp: Define invalid test data and give one example.

rubric.why: Identifies that boundary test data concerns the limits of the permitted input range.
rubric.description: States that boundary test data relates to the edges or limits of an input range.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the range limits.

rubric.why: Explains which values are tested at a boundary.
rubric.description: States that values at, just below, or just above the minimum or maximum are tested.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing the values tested.

modelAnswer: Boundary test data consists of values at the limits of the permitted input range, and values just below or just above those limits.
For example, if the valid range is 1 to 100, test 1 and 100, and values such as 0 and 101.
